sources_considered.why: Peer-reviewed theory paper (STOC 2024) on why calibrated pretrained models hallucinate.
OpenAI's explanation that hallucinations originate in next-word prediction pretraining.

receipt.public_excerpt: there is an inherent statistical lower-bound on the rate that pretrained language models hallucinate certain types of facts, having nothing to do with the transformer LM architecture or data quality.

evidence_items.explanation: Hallucination follows from statistical prediction itself, even with ideal data. That matches the claim that the generalizing process creates hallucinations.

evidence_items.locator: Section 'How hallucinations originate from next-word prediction'

receipt.public_excerpt: Spelling and parentheses follow consistent patterns, so errors there disappear with scale. But arbitrary low-frequency facts, like a pet’s birthday, cannot be predicted from patterns alone and hence lead to hallucinations.

evidence_items.explanation: OpenAI traces hallucinations to the pattern-based next-word prediction that makes models fluent, which supports the claim.

receipt.public_excerpt:
Claim: Hallucinations are inevitable.
Finding: They are not, because language models can abstain when uncertain.

evidence_items.explanation: This adds a caveat: post-training to abstain can reduce hallucinations. It does not deny that pretraining prediction creates them.

unresolved_gaps: Kalai and Vempala say pretraining gives no statistical reason for hallucinations on facts seen more than once or on systematic facts, so the link is strongest for rare, arbitrary facts.
